questions.prompt: The zeroes of the polynomial x² − 5x + 6 are

options.diagnosis: Found a factor pair of the constant term 6 but never checked the middle term: 1 + 6 = 7 ≠ 5.
Wrong factor pair AND wrong signs; expanding (x+1)(x+6) gives x² + 7x + 6, nothing like the original.

questions.explanation: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), so the zeroes are 2 and 3. Check with the coefficient relations: sum = 2 + 3 = 5 = −(−5)/1 ✓ and product = 6 = 6/1 ✓. Choosing −2, −3 reads the factors (x − 2)(x − 3) with flipped signs — substitute to verify: p(−2) = 4 + 10 + 6 = 20 ≠ 0.

questions.prompt: If α and β are the zeroes of 2x² − 7x + 3, then α + β equals

options.diagnosis: Reported the PRODUCT of the zeroes (c/a) instead of the sum.
Used −b but forgot to divide by a = 2; the relations are −b/a and c/a, not −b and c.

questions.explanation: For ax² + bx + c, α + β = −b/a = −(−7)/2 = 7/2, and αβ = c/a = 3/2. (The zeroes are 3 and 1/2: sum 7/2 ✓, product 3/2 ✓.) The double negative in −(−7) is where the sign trap lives.

questions.prompt: A quadratic polynomial whose zeroes have sum 3 and product −10 is

options.diagnosis: Dropped the sign of the product: the constant term equals the product itself (−10), not its absolute value.
Swapped the roles of sum and product: the template is x² − (sum)x + (product).

questions.explanation: A quadratic with zeroes summing to S and multiplying to P is k[x² − Sx + P]. With S = 3, P = −10: x² − 3x − 10 = (x − 5)(x + 2), zeroes 5 and −2 (sum 3 ✓, product −10 ✓). Note where each number goes and with what sign — the sum enters negated, the product as-is.

nodes.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
nodes.description: Two conditions, two unknowns: a pair of linear equations is two lines on the same plane, and everything depends on how those lines relate — crossing (one solution), parallel (none), or coincident (infinitely many), which the coefficient ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, c₁/c₂ diagnose without drawing. You will solve systems by substitution and elimination and use them to crack age, cost, speed and fraction word problems — the single most examined chapter of Class 10 algebra.

chapters: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

learning_outcomes: Can classify a pair of linear equations as consistent (unique or infinite solutions) or inconsistent using coefficient ratios
Can solve a pair of linear equations by substitution and by elimination, choosing the more efficient method
Can interpret the solution graphically as the intersection of two lines
Can translate word problems (ages, costs, digits, speeds, fractions) into pairs of equations and solve them

misconceptions.description: Proportional x- and y-coefficients alone decide everything: parallel and coincident lines are the same case, and the constants don't matter.
misconceptions.signal: Sees a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ and immediately declares 'infinitely many solutions' (or 'no solution') without checking c₁/c₂.
misconceptions.remedy: Same slope, different story: graph 3x + 2y = 5 and 6x + 4y = 10 (same line — infinite solutions), then 3x + 2y = 5 and 6x + 4y = 7 (parallel — none). The constants decide whether the twin lines coincide or merely run alongside. Ratio table with all three ratios, always.

misconceptions.description: In elimination, subtraction applies only to the chosen variable — other terms keep their signs (sign errors when subtracting equations).
misconceptions.signal: Subtracting x + y = 14 from x − y = 4 produces −y − y = 4 − 14 but writes +2y or botches the constant side.
misconceptions.remedy: Bracket discipline: write the subtraction as (x − y) − (x + y) = 4 − 14 with full brackets, then distribute the minus through EVERY term. Alternatively teach 'multiply by −1 and add' to avoid subtraction entirely — addition is sign-safe.

misconceptions.description: Every pair of linear equations has exactly one solution.
misconceptions.signal: Grinds elimination on a parallel pair, reaches 0 = 3, and 'solves' onward or declares x = 3; never anticipates no-solution or infinite cases.
misconceptions.remedy: Interpret the degenerate endings, don't fear them: 0 = (nonzero) means the lines never meet (no solution); 0 = 0 means the equations were the same line (infinitely many). Connect each algebraic ending to its picture so the student can narrate what the algebra discovered.

real_world_hooks: Two friends' orders at a canteen: 5 samosas + 7 teas = ₹50, 7 samosas + 5 teas = ₹46 — find each price
Boat upstream/downstream and train speed-distance classics
Comparing mobile plans: fixed rent + per-GB rate — where do two plans cost the same?
Election seat arithmetic: two parties' seats satisfying a sum and a difference

questions.prompt: The solution of the pair x + y = 14 and x − y = 4 is

options.diagnosis: Assigned the two values to the wrong variables; check in the second equation: 5 − 9 = −4 ≠ 4.
Satisfied only the first equation (10 + 4 = 14) and stopped; a solution must satisfy BOTH equations (10 − 4 = 6 ≠ 4).
Split 14 equally using only the first equation; the second equation forces the two numbers to differ by 4.

questions.explanation: Add the equations: 2x = 18, so x = 9; then y = 14 − 9 = 5. Verify in BOTH: 9 + 5 = 14 ✓ and 9 − 5 = 4 ✓. Every candidate must pass both equations — that is what 'solution of a pair' means.

questions.prompt: For what value of k does the pair 3x + 2y = 5 and 6x + 4y = k have INFINITELY many solutions?

options.diagnosis: Kept the constant unchanged while the left side doubled; the entire equation must scale by the same factor, so 5 must become 10.
Inverted the condition: k ≠ 10 gives parallel lines and NO solution; coincident lines need all three ratios equal.

questions.explanation: Infinitely many solutions require coincident lines: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂, i.e. 3/6 = 2/4 = 5/k, giving k = 10 (the second equation is then exactly double the first). If k ≠ 10 the lines are parallel and distinct — no solution. The constants matter as much as the coefficients.

questions.prompt: 5 pencils and 7 pens together cost ₹50, while 7 pencils and 5 pens together cost ₹46. The cost of one pencil is

options.diagnosis: Solved correctly but reported the PEN's price; always re-read which quantity the question asks for.
Found pencil + pen = 8 (by adding the equations) and stopped one step short of separating the two prices.
Found pen − pencil = 2 (by subtracting the equations) and reported the difference as the price.

questions.explanation: Let pencil = p, pen = q: 5p + 7q = 50 and 7p + 5q = 46. Adding: 12p + 12q = 96 ⟹ p + q = 8. Subtracting: 2q − 2p = 4 ⟹ q − p = 2. So q = 5, p = 3: a pencil costs ₹3 (pen ₹5). Check: 5(3) + 7(5) = 50 ✓, 7(3) + 5(5) = 46 ✓.

nodes.title: Quadratic Equations: Factoring, Formula, Discriminant
nodes.description: When a problem multiplies an unknown by itself — areas, projectiles, speed-time — you get a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0. This node solves them three ways (factorisation, completing the square, and the quadratic formula) and reads the discriminant D = b² − 4ac as a forecast: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal roots, D < 0 no real roots. It is the first equation family where 'how many solutions?' becomes a serious question.
learning_outcomes: Can solve quadratic equations by factorisation using the zero-product principle
Can apply the quadratic formula accurately, including sign handling for negative b and c
Can compute the discriminant and state the nature of the roots without solving
Can model word problems (areas, ages, speed-time) as quadratic equations, solve, and reject inadmissible roots

misconceptions.description: A negative discriminant means the equation has no solution of any kind (rather than no REAL solution).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 'no solution exists' for D < 0; treats the problem as unsolvable/invalid rather than as having no real roots.
misconceptions.remedy: Precision of language now, payoff in Class 11: D < 0 means the parabola never touches the x-axis, so no REAL number works — but the complex numbers of Class 11 will solve exactly these. Have the student write 'no real roots' and sketch the floating parabola as the geometric meaning.

misconceptions.description: In the quadratic formula, b is substituted with its sign ignored: x = (b ± √D)/2a, or −b becomes −(−4) = −4.
misconceptions.signal: For 2x² − 4x + 3, starts the formula with −4 instead of +4; sign chaos inside b² − 4ac when c < 0.
misconceptions.remedy: Bracket substitution ritual: write x = (−( b ) ± √(( b )² − 4( a )( c )))/(2( a )) with empty brackets first, then fill each bracket with the SIGNED coefficient. Slow once, correct forever — most formula errors die at the bracket stage.

misconceptions.description: Dividing both sides by x is a safe simplification: x² = 6x becomes x = 6.
misconceptions.signal: Solves x² = 6x and reports only x = 6; cancels common variable factors in equations routinely.
misconceptions.remedy: Show the murdered root: x = 0 satisfies x² = 6x, but dividing by x silently assumed x ≠ 0. Teach the safe alternative as reflex: bring everything to one side and factor — x(x − 6) = 0 keeps both roots alive. Rule: never divide an equation by an expression that could be zero.

misconceptions.description: The zero-product principle works for any number: if pq = 12 then p = 12 or q = 12 (or p, q are a factor pair like 3 and 4).
misconceptions.signal: From (x − 1)(x − 2) = 12 concludes x − 1 = 12 or x − 2 = 12, or matches x − 1 = 3, x − 2 = 4.
misconceptions.remedy: Expose the special role of zero: 12 = 1×12 = 2×6 = 3×4 = ... (infinitely many splits), but a product is ZERO only when a factor is zero — that uniqueness is the whole trick. Correct procedure: expand, move 12 across, re-factor against zero.

real_world_hooks: A cricket ball's flight: when is it 20 m high? Two moments, one moment, or never — that's the discriminant talking
Designing a rectangular garden of fixed area with a fixed perimeter budget
Speed problems: a train covering 360 km at x km/h saves 48 minutes at x + 5 — quadratic in disguise
Profit optimisation: unit price vs units sold trading off into a quadratic

questions.prompt: The roots of x² − 7x + 12 = 0 are

options.diagnosis: Picked a factor pair of 12 without checking the sum: 2 + 6 = 8, but the middle coefficient needs 7.

questions.explanation: Find two numbers with product +12 and sum +7: that is 3 and 4. So x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0, giving x = 3 or x = 4. Both the product AND the sum must check out — a factor pair of 12 alone (like 2, 6 or 1, 12) is not enough.

questions.prompt: The nature of the roots of 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0 is

options.diagnosis: Likely a discriminant arithmetic slip landing on 0; carefully: D = (−4)² − 4(2)(3) = 16 − 24 = −8, which is negative, not zero.

options.text: The equation is meaningless and has no solution of any kind

questions.explanation: D = b² − 4ac = (−4)² − 4(2)(3) = 16 − 24 = −8 < 0, so there are NO REAL roots — the parabola y = 2x² − 4x + 3 floats entirely above the x-axis. Mishandling the sign of b or c (e.g. computing 16 + 24 = 40) falsely yields two distinct roots. And 'no real roots' is not 'no solution at all': complex roots exist and arrive in Class 11.

questions.prompt: The solution set of x² = 6x is

options.diagnosis: Spotted the obvious root x = 0 but never factored to find the partner root 6.
Misread the equation as x² = 6; the right side here is 6x, a term containing the variable.

questions.explanation: Bring everything to one side: x² − 6x = 0 ⟹ x(x − 6) = 0 ⟹ x = 0 or x = 6. Dividing both sides by x 'simplifies' to x = 6 but silently assumes x ≠ 0, destroying the root x = 0. Never divide an equation by an expression that might be zero — factor instead.

nodes.title: Arithmetic Progressions: nth Term and Sum
nodes.description: Add the same amount each step — salaries with fixed annual raises, theatre rows growing seat by seat, EMI schedules — and you get an arithmetic progression. This node nails the two master formulas: the nth term aₙ = a + (n−1)d and the sum Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n−1)d] = n/2(first + last), plus the art of recognising when a situation IS an AP and when it merely looks like one.
learning_outcomes: Can identify whether a sequence is an AP by checking for a constant common difference
Can compute any term of an AP using aₙ = a + (n−1)d, and solve for a, d or n given the others
Can compute the sum of the first n terms using both forms of the sum formula
Can model real situations (instalments, stacked rows, salary increments) as APs and answer questions about them

misconceptions.description: The nth term is a + nd — the off-by-one in (n − 1) is dropped.
misconceptions.signal: Computes the 10th term of 3, 7, 11, ... as 3 + 10(4) = 43 instead of 3 + 9(4) = 39.
misconceptions.remedy: Count the JUMPS, not the terms: from term 1 to term 10 there are 9 jumps of d. Walk a number line physically or on screen — the first term uses zero jumps, which is exactly why a₁ = a + 0·d forces (n−1). Verify formula answers against brute-force listing for small n.

misconceptions.description: The nth term and the sum of n terms are interchangeable — one formula fits both questions.
misconceptions.signal: Asked for S₁₅, computes a₁₅; asked for the 20th term, reports the total of 20 terms.
misconceptions.remedy: Physical contrast: aₙ is ONE brick (the height of row n); Sₙ is the WHOLE wall (all bricks so far). Highlight question stems — 'term' vs 'sum/total/altogether' — and have the student label which formula the stem calls for before computing anything.

misconceptions.description: Any sequence with a visible pattern is an AP.
misconceptions.signal: Applies AP formulas to 2, 4, 8, 16 (geometric) or 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 (Fibonacci); checks only the first difference.
misconceptions.remedy: Make 'check the difference TWICE' the entry ticket: compute a₂ − a₁ AND a₃ − a₂ (at least) before touching formulas. Contrast tables of an AP vs GP growing side by side — same start, wildly different futures — to embed that 'pattern' is not one thing.

real_world_hooks: The Gauss legend: summing 1 to 100 by pairing ends — the sum formula's origin story
EMI and recurring deposits: fixed monthly additions are APs in your bank account
Theatre and stadium seating: rows of 20, 22, 24... seats — how many in row 30, how many total?
Taxi fares (base + per km) and ladder rungs shortening by a fixed amount (an NCERT favourite)

questions.prompt: The 10th term of the AP 3, 7, 11, 15, ... is

options.diagnosis: Computed 10 × 4 and ignored the first term entirely; the formula is a + (n−1)d, not n × d.
Computed the 9 jumps (9 × 4 = 36) but forgot to add the starting term 3.

questions.explanation: a = 3, d = 4. a₁₀ = a + (10 − 1)d = 3 + 9 × 4 = 39. From the 1st to the 10th term there are only 9 jumps of 4 — using 10 jumps (3 + 40 = 43) is the classic off-by-one.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an arithmetic progression?

options.diagnosis: Squares have growing differences (3, 5, 7, ...); a nearly-constant-looking pattern still fails the constant-difference test.

questions.explanation: Simplify the surds: √2, 2√2, 3√2, 4√2 — consecutive differences are all √2, a genuine AP in disguise. 2, 4, 8, 16 multiplies by 2 (geometric); 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 adds the previous two (Fibonacci); 1, 4, 9, 16 has differences 3, 5, 7. 'Has a pattern' is not the test — 'constant difference' is.

questions.prompt: The sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 2, 5, 8, ... is

options.diagnosis: Dropped the ½ in n/2: computed 20 × [2a + 19d] instead of 10 × [2a + 19d].

questions.explanation: a = 2, d = 3, n = 20. S₂₀ = 20/2 × [2(2) + 19(3)] = 10 × [4 + 57] = 10 × 61 = 610. Using 20d instead of 19d gives 640 (off-by-one); 59 is just the 20th TERM a₂₀ = 2 + 57 — a single brick, not the wall; forgetting the ÷2 doubles everything to 1220.

nodes.title: Triangles: Similarity, Basic Proportionality Theorem, Pythagoras
nodes.description: Similar figures have the same shape at different sizes: angles match, and corresponding sides scale by one common ratio. This node proves the Basic Proportionality (Thales) Theorem — a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally — establishes the AA, SSS and SAS similarity criteria, and puts them to work, including in proofs and applications of the Pythagoras theorem. Similarity is the mathematics of maps, models, shadows and zoom.
learning_outcomes: Can state and apply the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its converse to compute segment lengths
Can prove triangles similar using AA, SSS or SAS similarity criteria with correct correspondence
Can compute unknown sides of similar triangles using the scale factor (multiplicative, not additive)
Can apply the Pythagoras theorem and its converse in computations and proofs

misconceptions.description: Similar means congruent — same shape implies same size, so corresponding sides are equal.
misconceptions.signal: Uses ΔABC ~ ΔDEF to conclude AB = DE; expects 'matching' triangles to be identical cutouts.
misconceptions.remedy: Photo zoom demo: the same photo at 100% and 150% — every angle identical, every length scaled by 1.5. Similarity preserves SHAPE (angles, ratios); congruence additionally preserves SIZE and is the special case where the scale factor is 1.

misconceptions.description: Areas of similar triangles scale like the sides: ratio of areas = ratio of sides.
misconceptions.signal: For a scale factor of 3, says the bigger triangle has 3 times the area (instead of 9).
misconceptions.remedy: Grid-paper tiling: draw a triangle, then its 2× enlargement, and physically tile the big one with copies of the small — exactly 4 fit. Area is two-dimensional, so it scales by the SQUARE of the ratio. Link to pizza pricing: a 12-inch is not 'twice' an 6-inch.

misconceptions.description: Scaling works by adding: if one side grew by 2 cm, every side grows by 2 cm (additive instead of multiplicative reasoning).
misconceptions.signal: Given AB = 4 → DE = 6, predicts BC = 6 → EF = 8 ('add 2 again') instead of 9 ('multiply by 3/2').
misconceptions.remedy: Stretch a photo by adding 2 cm to each dimension and watch faces distort — addition ruins shape; only multiplication preserves it. Convert every similarity problem to an explicit scale factor first (new/old = 6/4 = 1.5), then multiply each side by it.

misconceptions.description: Pythagorean quantities combine linearly: √(a² + b²) = a + b and √(c² − a²) = c − a.
misconceptions.signal: Ladder problem with hypotenuse 13, base 5: answers height = 13 − 5 = 8; or hypotenuse of legs 3, 4 as 7.
misconceptions.remedy: Numeric collision with the 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triples: 13 − 5 = 8 but the true height is 12; 3 + 4 = 7 but the true hypotenuse is 5. The theorem trades in AREAS of squares (draw them on the sides); take roots only after all squaring and adding/subtracting is done.

real_world_hooks: Measure a coconut tree's height from its shadow and yours — similar triangles, no climbing
Google Maps scale: 1 cm = 500 m is one giant similarity transformation
Cinema projection: the film frame and the screen are similar rectangles metres apart in size
Architecture models: a 1:100 scale model of a stadium, and why its lawn area is 1:10000

questions.prompt: ΔABC ~ ΔDEF with AB = 4 cm, DE = 6 cm and BC = 6 cm. Then EF equals

options.diagnosis: Paired the sides incorrectly (matched EF with AB instead of BC); correspondence follows the order of the vertices in the similarity statement.

questions.explanation: The scale factor from ΔABC to ΔDEF is DE/AB = 6/4 = 3/2. So EF = BC × 3/2 = 6 × 3/2 = 9 cm. Adding 2 (because 4 'became' 6) gives 8 — additive reasoning breaks shape; similarity always multiplies by the same ratio.

questions.prompt: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. If AD = 2 cm, DB = 3 cm and AE = 4 cm, then EC equals

options.diagnosis: Inverted one side of the proportion: solved AD/DB = EC/AE instead of AD/DB = AE/EC.
Found the whole side AC = 10 via AD/AB = AE/AC, then subtracted AD (2) instead of AE (4) to get EC = 8; the piece removed must come from the SAME side.

questions.explanation: By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, AD/DB = AE/EC: 2/3 = 4/EC ⟹ EC = 4 × 3/2 = 6 cm. The additive trap answers 5 (AD grew by 2 to give AE = 4, so DB 'should' grow by 2 to 5) — but proportionality multiplies (AE = 2 × AD, so EC = 2 × DB = 6).

questions.prompt: A 13 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 5 m from the wall's base. The height at which the ladder touches the wall is

options.diagnosis: Added the squares (169 + 25) instead of subtracting; the ladder is the HYPOTENUSE, so the wall height is a leg: √(13² − 5²).

questions.explanation: The wall, ground and ladder form a right triangle with hypotenuse 13 (the ladder) and base 5. Height = √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 m. Computing 13 − 5 = 8 or 13 + 5 = 18 treats square roots linearly — Pythagoras works with squared lengths, and the root comes last.

nodes.title: Coordinate Geometry: Distance, Section Formula, Areas
nodes.description: Once points have coordinates, geometry becomes computation. The distance formula (Pythagoras in disguise) measures lengths, the section formula finds the point dividing a segment in a given ratio (midpoint as the friendly special case), and a determinant-style formula computes triangle areas — including the test for three points lying on one line. This node turns classification problems ('is this a rhombus?') into arithmetic.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the distance between two points and use it to classify triangles and quadrilaterals
Can apply the section formula to find a point dividing a segment in ratio m:n, and the midpoint as a special case
Can find the area of a triangle from its vertices and use area = 0 as a collinearity test
Can solve reverse problems: find a coordinate or ratio given a distance, midpoint or section condition

misconceptions.description: Distance combines linearly: √((Δx)² + (Δy)²) is computed as Δx + Δy, or the square root is skipped.
misconceptions.signal: Distance from (0,0) to (3,4) reported as 7 (adding legs) or 25 (forgetting the root).
misconceptions.remedy: Reconnect the formula to its picture: draw the right triangle with legs Δx and Δy — the distance is its hypotenuse, and 3-4-5 is the sanity check. Insist on the final unit check: a 'distance' of 25 between points 3 and 4 apart fails the smell test.

misconceptions.description: The midpoint is found by adding coordinates (without dividing by 2), or the given ratio can be ignored when sectioning.
misconceptions.signal: Midpoint of (2,3) and (6,7) reported as (8,10); uses the midpoint formula on a 2:1 section problem.
misconceptions.remedy: Midpoint as average: it must lie BETWEEN the endpoints, so each coordinate is the mean of the two. Plot the answer — (8,10) sits far outside the segment, an instant visual veto. For sections, ratio ≠ 1:1 means the point slides toward one end; the midpoint formula is only the 1:1 case.

misconceptions.description: In the section formula, the ratio m:n attaches to the wrong endpoints (m weights the near end instead of the far end).
misconceptions.signal: For P dividing AB in 2:1, computes (2·A + 1·B)/3 instead of (2·B + 1·A)/3; answers land nearer the wrong endpoint.
misconceptions.remedy: Cross-weighting mnemonic with a picture: the point sits closer to the endpoint with the SMALLER share, and each endpoint is multiplied by the ratio part belonging to the OTHER side (m multiplies x₂). Always predict roughly where P should sit before computing, then let the prediction police the formula.

real_world_hooks: Food delivery apps compute rider-to-restaurant distances from map coordinates
Dividing a straight road between two towns in a 2:1 ratio to place a toll booth
GPS surveying of a triangular plot: its area straight from corner coordinates
Game development: hit detection and spawn points are distance-formula arithmetic

questions.prompt: The distance between the points (0, 0) and (3, 4) is

options.diagnosis: Added the differences BEFORE squaring: computed √(3 + 4) instead of √(3² + 4²).

questions.explanation: Distance = √((3−0)² + (4−0)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 — the classic 3-4-5 right triangle. Adding the legs (7) or stopping at 25 (no root) are the two standard slips; both are caught by remembering the formula IS Pythagoras.

questions.prompt: The midpoint of the segment joining (2, 3) and (6, 7) is

options.diagnosis: Computed the half-DIFFERENCES ((6−2)/2, (7−3)/2) — that is half the displacement, not the midpoint's location.
Averaged correctly but swapped the x- and y-coordinates when writing the answer.

questions.explanation: Midpoint = ((2+6)/2, (3+7)/2) = (4, 5) — the average of each coordinate. (8, 10) forgets the division and lands outside the segment entirely; a midpoint must sit between its endpoints, which makes this error visually obvious on a sketch.

questions.prompt: The point P divides the segment from A(2, −2) to B(−7, 4) in the ratio 2:1 (i.e. AP:PB = 2:1). The coordinates of P are

options.diagnosis: Sign slips while combining the negative coordinates; recompute (2(−7) + 1(2))/3 = −4 and (2(4) + 1(−2))/3 = 2 carefully.

questions.explanation: Section formula: P = ((m·x₂ + n·x₁)/(m+n), (m·y₂ + n·y₁)/(m+n)) with m:n = 2:1, A = (x₁,y₁), B = (x₂,y₂). P = ((2(−7) + 1(2))/3, (2(4) + 1(−2))/3) = (−12/3, 6/3) = (−4, 2). Reversing the ratio gives (−1, 0), which sits closer to A — but AP:PB = 2:1 forces P to sit closer to B. The midpoint (−5/2, 1) ignores the ratio altogether.

nodes.title: Circles: Tangents and Their Properties
nodes.description: A tangent kisses a circle at exactly one point — and at that point it stands perfectly perpendicular to the radius. From this single fact plus congruence comes the second gem: the two tangents drawn from an external point are equal in length. This short, elegant node proves both theorems and applies them to compute lengths and angles in tangent configurations, from bicycle chains to belt drives.
learning_outcomes: Can define a tangent and distinguish it from a secant and a chord
Can apply the theorem 'the tangent at any point is perpendicular to the radius through that point' in computations
Can prove and use the equality of the two tangent lengths from an external point
Can solve mixed problems combining tangents with Pythagoras and angle-chasing (e.g. the angle between two tangents)

misconceptions.description: The two tangent segments from an external point have different lengths (their equality is not known or not trusted).
misconceptions.signal: Computes each tangent length separately and expects different answers; cannot justify PA = PB.
misconceptions.remedy: Prove it with RHS congruence: triangles OAP and OBP share hypotenuse OP, have equal radii OA = OB, and right angles at the contact points — so PA = PB. Physical anchor: a string looped from your finger around a bangle pulls equally on both sides.

misconceptions.description: The radius-tangent right angle is forgotten or misplaced (the right angle is put at the centre or the external point).
misconceptions.signal: In tangent-length problems, applies Pythagoras with OP as a leg instead of the hypotenuse; adds squares when they should be subtracted.
misconceptions.remedy: Always draw and MARK the right angle at the point of contact before any computation — the triangle O-contact-external has its hypotenuse OP opposite that right angle. One marked figure eliminates the entire family of errors.

misconceptions.description: A tangent may cut the circle at two points, or any line touching 'near the edge' is a tangent (tangent/secant confusion).
misconceptions.signal: Draws 'tangents' that visibly cross the circle; counts a secant's two intersections as two tangent points.
misconceptions.remedy: Slide a secant outward interactively: its two intersection points glide together and fuse into one at the moment of tangency. Definition sharpened by the motion: tangent = the limiting position of a secant, meeting the circle at exactly one point.

real_world_hooks: A bicycle chain runs along the common tangents of the two gear circles
A stone released from a sling flies off along the tangent — not along the radius
Belt drives in flour mills and motors: tangent lengths decide belt sizes
A ladder grazing a circular water tank touches it at exactly one point

questions.prompt: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point OUTSIDE the circle?

options.diagnosis: Confused with a point ON the circle, where exactly one tangent exists; from outside, one tangent grazes each 'side' of the circle.
Possibly confused with a point INSIDE the circle, from which no tangent can be drawn (every line through it is a secant).

questions.explanation: From an external point exactly two tangents touch the circle, one on each side, and their lengths are equal. From a point on the circle: exactly one. From inside: none, since every line through an interior point must cross the circle twice.

questions.prompt: From a point P, 25 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 7 cm, the length of the tangent PA is

options.diagnosis: Computed 25 − 7 linearly; Pythagoras subtracts SQUARES (625 − 49), not lengths.
Assumed the tangent length equals the radius; the tangent segment runs from P to the contact point and depends on how far P is from the centre.

questions.explanation: OA ⊥ PA at the contact point A, so ΔOAP is right-angled at A with hypotenuse OP = 25 and leg OA = 7. PA = √(25² − 7²) = √(625 − 49) = √576 = 24 cm. Adding squares (√674) misplaces the right angle — it sits at A, making OP the hypotenuse.

questions.prompt: Tangents TP and TQ are drawn from an external point T, touching the circle with centre O at P and Q. If ∠PTQ = 60°, then ∠POQ equals

options.diagnosis: Halved instead of supplementing; the centre-circumference doubling rule doesn't apply to the tangent configuration — quadrilateral angle sum does.
Assumed the angle at the centre is always right; the right angles here are at P and Q, the contact points, not at O.

questions.explanation: In quadrilateral TPOQ, the angles at P and Q are 90° each (radius ⊥ tangent). So ∠PTQ + ∠POQ = 360° − 90° − 90° = 180°: they are supplementary, giving ∠POQ = 180° − 60° = 120°. Forgetting the two right angles leads to guessing ∠POQ = ∠PTQ.

nodes.title: Constructions: Dividing Segments and Drawing Tangents
nodes.description: Class 10 constructions are applied similarity and circle theory: divide a segment in any given ratio m:n, construct a triangle similar to a given one with a given scale factor, and draw the pair of tangents to a circle from an external point. Each construction must be justified — the parallel-line division leans on the Basic Proportionality Theorem, and the tangent construction leans on the angle in a semicircle being 90°.
learning_outcomes: Can divide a line segment internally in a given ratio m:n and justify the construction using the Basic Proportionality Theorem
Can construct a triangle similar to a given triangle with a given scale factor (both smaller and larger than 1)
Can construct the pair of tangents to a circle from an external point and justify why the construction works
Can explain each construction's justification rather than merely reproduce its steps

misconceptions.description: To divide a segment in ratio m:n, mark m (or n, or max(m,n)) equally spaced points on the auxiliary ray instead of m + n.
misconceptions.signal: For ratio 3:5 marks 5 points and joins the 3rd; the resulting pieces measure to a wrong ratio.
misconceptions.remedy: Reason from the goal backwards: the ratio 3:5 splits the segment into 3 + 5 = 8 equal shares, so the ray needs 8 equal steps with the join at step 3. Verify one construction with a ruler after completing it legally — the measured 3:5 makes the m+n rule stick.

misconceptions.description: A scale factor like 3/5 produces a LARGER triangle (or 5/3 a smaller one) — the fraction's size relative to 1 is ignored.
misconceptions.signal: Asked for a 3/5-scale similar triangle, extends the sides beyond the original; surprises at the result's size.
misconceptions.remedy: Pre-commit to the outcome before constructing: 3/5 < 1 means every side shrinks (predict: inside the original); 5/3 > 1 means each side stretches (predict: outside). Comparing the finished figure with the prediction closes the loop; connect to photo zoom percentages (60% vs 166%).

misconceptions.description: Constructions are validated by measuring the result; the justification step is decorative.
misconceptions.signal: When asked WHY the tangent construction works, answers 'because it looks/measures right'; skips justification in exams.
misconceptions.remedy: Flip the exercise: present a slightly wrong construction that measures 'close enough' and ask whether it is valid. Only the deductive justification (BPT for division; semicircle angle for tangents) can tell exact from approximately right — that is precisely why boards award marks for it.

real_world_hooks: A tailor divides cloth in 3:5 with folds and a straight edge — no calculator, pure geometry
Scale factors in tailoring patterns: grading a size M design up to XL
Architects' reductions: redrawing a site plan at 3/5 scale by construction, pre-CAD
Pipeline to a circular tank: the approach lines are exactly the external tangents

questions.prompt: To divide a segment AB in the ratio 3:5 by the standard construction, the minimum number of equally spaced points to mark on the ray AX is

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 3 × 5; the ratio's parts are ADDED (3 + 5 shares), not multiplied.

questions.explanation: A 3:5 split cuts AB into 3 + 5 = 8 equal shares, so mark 8 equal steps A₁...A₈ on the ray, join A₈ to B, and draw the parallel through A₃. The BPT then guarantees the pieces of AB are in ratio 3:5.

questions.prompt: A triangle is constructed similar to ΔABC with scale factor 3/5. The new triangle is

options.text: Smaller than ΔABC — each side is 3/5 of the corresponding side

options.diagnosis: Treats 'similar' as 'identical'; the scale factor 3/5 ≠ 1 explicitly changes every length while preserving angles.

options.text: Impossible to construct, since 3/5 is less than 1
options.diagnosis: Believes only enlargements can be constructed; reductions use the same parallel-line method with the join at the 3rd of 5 marks.

questions.explanation: A scale factor compares new to old: 3/5 < 1 shrinks every side to 3/5 of the original (angles unchanged). A factor like 5/3 > 1 would enlarge. Both directions use the same ray-and-parallels construction; only the mark you join through changes.

questions.prompt: In constructing tangents from an external point P to a circle with centre O, we bisect OP at M and draw a circle with centre M and radius MO. Why?

options.text: Any point A where this circle meets the given circle satisfies ∠OAP = 90° (angle in a semicircle), making PA perpendicular to radius OA — hence a tangent
Because the new circle has the same radius as the given circle
options.diagnosis: The auxiliary circle's radius is OP/2, unrelated to the given circle's radius; its job is to create a semicircle on diameter OP.

options.text: Because bisecting OP always makes arcs intersect more accurately
Because each tangent's length equals OP/2
options.diagnosis: The tangent length is √(OP² − r²), not OP/2; the half-length belongs to the auxiliary circle's radius, not to the tangents.

questions.explanation: The circle on diameter OP passes through every point A at which ∠OAP = 90° (angle in a semicircle). Where it cuts the given circle, OA is a radius AND OA ⊥ AP — exactly the tangency condition. The construction manufactures the right angle; the justification is the semicircle theorem, not measurement.

nodes.title: Introduction to Trigonometry: Ratios and Identities
nodes.description: Trigonometry begins with a right triangle and one acute angle: the ratios of its sides — sine, cosine, tangent and their reciprocals — depend only on the angle, not on the triangle's size. This node defines the six ratios, computes exact values at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, and proves and applies the fundamental identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and its companions. These ratios are how astronomers measured the unreachable — and how you will, too.
learning_outcomes: Can define sin, cos, tan (and their reciprocals) for an acute angle of a right triangle and compute them from given sides
Can recall and use the exact values of the trigonometric ratios at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°
Can find the remaining ratios when one ratio is given, using Pythagoras
Can prove and apply the identities sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ

misconceptions.description: Trigonometric ratios scale linearly with the angle: sin 60° = 2 × sin 30°.
misconceptions.signal: Computes sin 60° as 1; interpolates sin 45° as the average of sin 30° and sin 60°.
misconceptions.remedy: Numeric collision: sin 30° = 0.5 but sin 60° ≈ 0.866 ≠ 1, and sin 90° = 1 ≠ 2 × sin 45° ≈ 1.414. Show the unit-circle/half-chord picture: sine grows as a CURVE that flattens near 90°, not as a straight line through angle values.

misconceptions.description: The ratio definitions are interchangeable or misassigned: sin is adjacent/hypotenuse, tan is opposite/hypotenuse, etc.
misconceptions.signal: For a 7-24-25 triangle writes sin A = 24/25 when the side opposite A is 7; answers cos when sin is asked.
misconceptions.remedy: Label before you compute: mark the angle, then physically label Opposite, Adjacent, Hypotenuse on the figure for THAT angle (the labels move if the angle moves!). SOH-CAH-TOA only after the labelling ritual; follow with mixed drills where the marked angle switches vertex.

misconceptions.description: 'sin' is a quantity that multiplies θ, so it can be cancelled: sin 60°/sin 30° = 60/30 = 2.
misconceptions.signal: Cancels sin across fractions; writes sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B; treats sin θ/θ as sin.
misconceptions.remedy: Attack the notation head-on: sin is a FUNCTION (a machine), not a factor — 'sin 30°' means 'the machine's output at 30°', like f(30). Counterexample battery: sin 60°/sin 30° = √3 ≠ 2; sin(30°+60°) = 1 ≠ sin 30° + sin 60° ≈ 1.37.

misconceptions.description: Trigonometric ratios depend on the triangle's size: a bigger right triangle has bigger sines.
misconceptions.signal: Recomputes sin 30° for a 'larger' triangle expecting a different value; distrusts tables for triangles of unstated size.
misconceptions.remedy: Similarity is the reason trig works: nest several right triangles sharing the same acute angle (same shape, different sizes) and compute opposite/hypotenuse in each — the ratio is identical every time. This is exactly why the ratio deserves a name that mentions only the ANGLE.

real_world_hooks: Aryabhata's jya (half-chord) tables from 499 CE — 'sine' is a mistranslation journey from Sanskrit through Arabic to Latin
A wheelchair ramp's legal steepness is a tangent ratio in disguise
Carrom and snooker angle shots: aiming is applied tangent
Smartphone tilt sensors report your phone's angle via trig ratios

questions.prompt: The value of sin 30° is

options.diagnosis: Recalled the 45° value; in the special-values table sin 45° = 1/√2, while sin 30° = 1/2.

questions.explanation: In a 30-60-90 triangle the side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse, so sin 30° = 1/2. √3/2 is cos 30° (or sin 60°) — the classic swap. 1/3 comes from treating the ratio as 30/90, i.e. reading 'sin' as something you can strip away from the angle.

questions.prompt: If tan θ = 3/4 for an acute angle θ, then sin θ equals

options.diagnosis: Computed cos θ (adjacent/hypotenuse) instead of sin θ; both new ratios use the hypotenuse 5, but sine takes the OPPOSITE side 3.
Inverted the ratio — hypotenuse over opposite is cosec θ, and a sine of an acute angle can never exceed 1.

questions.explanation: tan θ = opposite/adjacent = 3/4, so build the right triangle with legs 3 and 4: hypotenuse = √(9+16) = 5. Then sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse = 3/5 (and cos θ = 4/5). Reusing 3/4 for sine ignores that sine's denominator is the hypotenuse, not the adjacent side.

questions.prompt: A student claims: 'sin 60° = 2 × sin 30°, because 60° is twice 30°.' This claim is

options.text: False: sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87, while 2 × sin 30° = 1 — sine does not scale linearly with the angle
True, because doubling the angle doubles the opposite side
True, and sin 90° = 2 × sin 45° confirms it
options.diagnosis: The 'confirmation' fails: sin 90° = 1 but 2 × sin 45° = √2 ≈ 1.41; testing the pattern on another pair would have refuted it.

options.text: False for small triangles but true for large ones

questions.explanation: Check the values: sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866 and 2 sin 30° = 2 × 1/2 = 1. Not equal — sine is not proportional to the angle (the sine curve bends and flattens toward 90°). And triangle size is irrelevant: similar triangles give the same ratios, which is the entire reason sin 30° is a single well-defined number.

nodes.title: Applications of Trigonometry: Heights and Distances
nodes.description: How tall is the tower you cannot climb, how far the ship you cannot reach? Stand somewhere, measure an angle of elevation or depression, and let trigonometry do the climbing. This node turns word descriptions into right-triangle diagrams, chooses the ratio that links the known and unknown sides (usually tan), and solves single- and double-triangle problems — the survey engineer's daily bread since long before lasers.
learning_outcomes: Can define and correctly place angles of elevation and depression in a diagram, both measured from the HORIZONTAL
Can draw a correct right-triangle model from a verbal description, including observer height when given
Can choose the appropriate trigonometric ratio and compute heights and distances using exact values (30°, 45°, 60°)
Can solve two-triangle problems (two observation points, or two objects) by combining equations

misconceptions.description: The angle of depression is measured from the vertical (or drawn inside the wrong triangle), instead of down from the horizontal.
misconceptions.signal: From a 75 m tower with 30° depression, computes the distance as 75 tan 30° instead of 75/tan 30°; diagrams show the angle at the base of the tower.
misconceptions.remedy: Always draw the horizontal eye-line first, then swing DOWN from it for depression (and up for elevation). Use the alternate-angle shortcut: the depression at the top equals the elevation from the object — re-locating the angle inside the ground triangle prevents the vertical-reference error.

misconceptions.description: Any trigonometric ratio works: sin/cos/tan are chosen by habit rather than by which sides are involved.
misconceptions.signal: Uses sin for opposite/adjacent situations; for a 30 m baseline and 30° elevation writes h = 30 sin 30°.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the three-question ritual before computing: Which side do I KNOW? Which do I WANT? Which ratio links exactly those two? (tan for the two legs; sin/cos only when the hypotenuse — a slant like a string or ladder — is involved.) Label O/A/H on every diagram relative to the marked angle.

misconceptions.description: The slant distance and the horizontal distance are the same thing (string length = ground distance; line-of-sight = horizontal).
misconceptions.signal: Treats a 60 m kite string as the horizontal leg; reports the line-of-sight distance when the question asks the horizontal one.
misconceptions.remedy: Colour-code the triangle: hypotenuse (string, ladder, line of sight) in one colour, legs (height, ground distance) in another, and name each in words before computing. A quick reality check helps: the slant is always the LONGEST of the three.

real_world_hooks: Measure the height of the Qutub Minar from the ground with a clinometer made from a protractor, straw and thread
Lighthouse keepers judging a ship's distance from the angle of depression
Aircraft descent: pilots fly a 3° glide slope — pure tangent arithmetic
Mountain surveying: how the height of Mount Everest was first computed from plains far away

questions.prompt: From a point 30 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of its top is 30°. The height of the tower is

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by tan 60° instead of tan 30° — or inverted the tangent ratio; check: height = (base) × tan 30° = 30/√3.
Assumed height = distance, which happens only at 45° elevation; at 30° the tower is shorter than the baseline.

questions.explanation: tan 30° = height/30, so height = 30 × tan 30° = 30 × (1/√3) = 10√3 ≈ 17.3 m. Using sin 30° gives 15 (wrong ratio: sine needs the hypotenuse, but 30 m is the horizontal LEG); 30√3 comes from using tan 60°, i.e. placing the angle at the top instead of the observation point.

questions.prompt: A kite flies at the end of a taut 60 m string that makes 60° with the ground. The height of the kite above the ground is

options.diagnosis: Divided by tan 60° (60/√3), treating the string as the horizontal base and the ratio as tangent — two setup errors stacked.

questions.explanation: The string is the HYPOTENUSE, so height = 60 × sin 60° = 60 × (√3/2) = 30√3 ≈ 52 m. Using tan (60 × √3 = 60√3 ≈ 104 m) treats the 60 m string as the horizontal leg — but the string is the slant, and no leg can exceed it. 60 × cos 60° = 30 computes the horizontal distance, not the height.

questions.prompt: From the top of a 75 m high lighthouse, the angle of depression of a ship is 30°. The horizontal distance of the ship from the lighthouse is

options.diagnosis: Assumed distance = height, true only for a 45° angle; at a shallow 30° depression the ship is much farther out.

questions.explanation: The 30° depression from the top equals the 30° elevation from the ship (alternate angles). tan 30° = 75/d, so d = 75/tan 30° = 75√3 ≈ 130 m. Computing 75 × tan 30° = 25√3 measures the angle from the vertical — the depression-from-horizontal error. 75/sin 30° = 150 m is the slant line-of-sight distance, not the horizontal one.

nodes.title: Areas Related to Circles: Sectors and Segments
nodes.description: A sector is a pizza slice, a segment is what a chord cuts off. This node computes arc lengths and sector areas as fractions (θ/360) of the whole circle's circumference and area, finds segment areas by subtracting the triangle from its sector, and handles combinations — flower beds on square lawns, wiper sweeps, and designs of overlapping circles. One idea powers it all: an angle's share of 360° is its share of the circle.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the arc length of a sector as (θ/360) × 2πr and its area as (θ/360) × πr²
Can compute the perimeter of a sector (arc + two radii), distinguishing it from the arc length
Can compute the area of a minor segment as sector area minus triangle area
Can solve combination problems: sweeps of wiper blades, designs from squares and circles, grazing regions

misconceptions.description: The circumference and area formulas are interchangeable inside the sector fraction: (θ/360) × 2πr computes area, or (θ/360) × πr² computes arc length.
misconceptions.signal: Reports an 'arc length' with cm² character (uses r²), or a tiny 'area' that is really a length.
misconceptions.remedy: Unit-first discipline: lengths must come from 2πr (single r), areas from πr² (r squared) — check the exponent of r against the units of the answer before accepting it. The fraction θ/360 is the same in both; only the base quantity changes.

misconceptions.description: The segment IS the sector — the triangle need not be subtracted.
misconceptions.signal: For a 90° segment reports (90/360)πr² and stops; diagrams shade the full slice instead of the chord's cap.
misconceptions.remedy: Shade-and-cut: draw the sector, draw the chord, and physically cut away the triangle — what remains in hand is the segment. Formula follows the scissors: segment = sector − triangle. Insist the student sketch and shade the target region before computing anything.

misconceptions.description: The perimeter of a sector equals its arc length (the two radii are forgotten), or conversely radii are added when only the arc is asked.
misconceptions.signal: Fencing a pizza-slice garden but buying fence only for the curved edge; adds 2r when the question says 'length of the arc'.
misconceptions.remedy: Finger-trace the boundary: perimeter means walking the FULL boundary — along one radius, around the arc, back down the other radius (arc + 2r). Contrast with 'arc length', which is only the curved part. The tracing habit resolves every such ambiguity.

real_world_hooks: Pizza and paratha slices: is a 90° slice of a 7-inch really smaller than a 60° slice of a 9-inch?
Car wiper blades sweep circular sectors — how much windscreen do they clean?
A goat tethered at the corner of a square field: the grazing region is a sector
Athletics tracks and cricket boundary arcs: curved-length calculations in sports design

questions.prompt: The area of a sector of a circle of radius 6 cm with central angle 60° is

options.diagnosis: Computed the FULL circle's area, forgetting the sector fraction θ/360 = 1/6.
Used θ/180 instead of θ/360 — halving the circle instead of taking the angle's true share of 360°.

questions.explanation: Sector area = (θ/360) × πr² = (60/360) × π × 36 = 6π cm² (≈ 18.85). Using 2πr instead of πr² gives 2π — that is the ARC LENGTH formula and even carries the wrong units (cm, not cm²).

questions.prompt: A sector of a circle of radius 21 cm has central angle 60°. The length of its arc is (take π = 22/7)

options.diagnosis: Computed the full circumference 2πr and forgot to take the 60/360 share of it.

questions.explanation: Arc = (θ/360) × 2πr = (60/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 21 = (1/6) × 132 = 22 cm. The area formula with the same fraction gives 231 cm² — a different quantity with different units. 64 cm is the sector's PERIMETER (22 + 21 + 21), which includes the two radii; the arc alone is just the curve.

questions.prompt: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre. The area of the minor SEGMENT is

options.diagnosis: Computed only the TRIANGLE'S area (½ × 10 × 10) — that is the part removed, not the segment that remains.
Subtracted the triangle from the FULL circle instead of from the 90° sector; the sector fraction 90/360 was skipped.

questions.explanation: Sector (90°) area = (90/360) × π × 100 = 25π. Triangle formed by the two radii and the chord is right-angled at the centre: area = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50. Minor segment = sector − triangle = 25π − 50 ≈ 28.5 cm². The segment is what lies between the chord and the arc — always the slice MINUS the triangle.

nodes.title: Surface Areas and Volumes: Combined Solids
nodes.description: Real objects are combinations: a capsule is a cylinder with hemispherical ends, an ice-cream cone is a cone crowned by a hemisphere, a tent is a cylinder wearing a conical hat. This node computes surface areas of such composites (counting only the surfaces that actually show — glued faces vanish) and their volumes (which simply add), including melt-and-recast problems where one shape's volume becomes another's. It is Class 9 mensuration graduating into engineering.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the surface area of a combined solid by summing only the EXPOSED surfaces of each component
Can compute the volume of a combined solid by adding component volumes
Can solve conversion problems (melting, recasting, pouring) using conservation of volume
Can select the correct component formulas (CSA vs TSA, hemisphere vs sphere) for each part of a composite

misconceptions.description: The surface area of a combined solid is the sum of the TOTAL surface areas of its components — glued, hidden faces included.
misconceptions.signal: For a cone on a hemisphere adds TSA(cone) + TSA(hemisphere), double-counting the joint circle twice over.
misconceptions.remedy: Paint test: imagine dipping the toy in paint — which surfaces get wet? The two glued circular faces meet inside and get no paint. Rule extracted: composite surface = sum of EXPOSED parts only (usually the curved surfaces plus any genuinely open flat faces).

misconceptions.description: Surface area and volume formulas are interchangeable when convenient (4πr² used for volume, πr²h for a surface).
misconceptions.signal: In a melt-and-recast problem equates surface areas; answers carry mismatched units (cm² for a capacity).
misconceptions.remedy: Dimension gate before every substitution: volume formulas contain three length factors (r³ or r²h), area formulas two. Melting conserves the AMOUNT of material — a volume — never the surface (a crushed laddoo has the same volume but new surface). Attach units through the computation once to make it visceral.

misconceptions.description: Melting or recasting changes the amount of material — volume is not conserved, so such problems 'cannot be solved'.
misconceptions.signal: Refuses to equate the sphere's and cylinder's volumes; adds a fudge factor for 'material lost in melting'.
misconceptions.remedy: Clay-in-hand demonstration: reshape a clay ball into a snake — nothing added, nothing removed, volume identical while shape and surface change wildly. Idealisation made explicit: board problems assume no wastage, so V(before) = V(after) is exactly the equation to write.

real_world_hooks: Medicine capsules: cylinder + two hemispheres — compute the gelatin needed
A circus tent: cylindrical walls with a conical roof — canvas is CSA only, no floor, no ceiling
Melting old silver bangles into a new idol: volume conservation at the jeweller's
Ice-cream cones with a hemispherical scoop: how much ice-cream, how much wafer?

questions.prompt: A toy is a cone mounted on a hemisphere of the same radius (bases glued together). The total surface area of the toy equals

options.text: CSA of cone + CSA of hemisphere
TSA of cone + TSA of hemisphere
CSA of cone + CSA of hemisphere + area of the common circle
options.diagnosis: Added the glued junction circle back in; that circle is buried inside the toy and shows on neither surface.

options.text: Volume of cone + volume of hemisphere

questions.explanation: Only exposed surfaces count: the cone shows its curved surface (πrl) and the hemisphere its curved surface (2πr²); their flat circular faces are glued face-to-face inside the toy and vanish from view. Adding TSAs would count that hidden circle twice — once from each solid.

questions.prompt: A metallic sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into a cylinder of radius 6 cm. The height of the cylinder is

options.diagnosis: Used 4πr³ for the sphere — dropped the ⅓ in 4/3; the sphere formula is (4/3)πr³.

options.text: It cannot be determined, because melting changes the amount of metal

questions.explanation: Melting conserves volume: (4/3)π(6)³ = π(6)²h ⟹ (4/3)(216) = 36h ⟹ 288 = 36h ⟹ h = 8 cm. Using the sphere's surface area 4πr² in place of its volume (4π(36) = π(36)h) gives h = 4 — an area equated to a volume; surfaces are not conserved when reshaping, only the metal's volume is.

questions.prompt: A solid toy is a cone of height 4 cm and radius 3 cm mounted on a hemisphere of radius 3 cm. The volume of the toy is

options.diagnosis: Used the FULL sphere volume (4/3)π(27) = 36π for the bottom piece instead of the hemisphere's half, 18π.
Dropped the ⅓ in the cone's volume: computed π(9)(4) = 36π for the cone instead of 12π.
Used (1/3)πr³ = 9π for the hemisphere — mixing the cone's ⅓ into the hemisphere's formula, which is (2/3)πr³.

questions.explanation: Volumes of components simply add: cone = ⅓π(3²)(4) = 12π; hemisphere = (2/3)π(3³) = 18π. Total = 12π + 18π = 30π cm³ ≈ 94.3 cm³. Each solid keeps its own formula — ⅓ belongs to the cone, 2/3 to the hemisphere, and the glued faces are irrelevant to volume.

nodes.title: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode of Grouped Data; Ogives
nodes.description: When data arrives pre-grouped into classes, the exact values are gone — so mean, median and mode must be estimated from the group structure: mean via class marks weighted by frequencies, median via the cumulative-frequency formula (or read off an ogive), and mode via the modal-class formula. This node teaches all three, the empirical bridge mode ≈ 3(median) − 2(mean), and when each measure is the right summary to report.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the mean of grouped data by the direct and assumed-mean methods using class marks and frequencies
Can identify the modal class and median class of a grouped distribution
Can compute the median of grouped data with the formula, and read it from an ogive at n/2
Can apply the empirical relationship mode = 3(median) − 2(mean) and judge which average best represents a dataset

misconceptions.description: The mean of grouped data is the plain average of the class marks — frequencies play no role.
misconceptions.signal: Adds up the class marks, divides by the number of classes; a heavily-populated class moves the answer not at all.
misconceptions.remedy: Break it with a lopsided example: 98 students score around 5 and 2 students around 95 — averaging the class marks says 50, which describes nobody. Each class mark must be WEIGHTED by how many people it represents: mean = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ. The word 'weighted' should trigger the frequency column.

misconceptions.description: The mode of grouped data is the largest frequency itself (or the class mark of any big class), not a value located inside the modal class.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'mode = 12' when 12 is the highest FREQUENCY; confuses the count of observations with their value.
misconceptions.remedy: Separate the two axes verbally: frequency says HOW MANY, the mode says WHICH VALUE occurs most. First point at the modal class (the tallest histogram bar), then use the formula to locate the peak inside it. Asking 'mode = 12 what? 12 students or 12 marks?' usually exposes and repairs the confusion.

misconceptions.description: The median from an ogive (or formula) is read at n rather than n/2, or cumulative frequency is treated like ordinary frequency.
misconceptions.signal: Reads the ogive at the topmost point (x where cf = n); uses a plain frequency in place of 'cf of preceding class' in the formula.
misconceptions.remedy: Reconnect to the meaning: the median is the value with HALF the data below it, so the ogive must be read at height n/2 — the top of the curve is where ALL the data lies below, which is just the maximum. Trace with a ruler: horizontal at n/2, drop vertical, read x.

real_world_hooks: Board-exam result analysis: your school's grouped marks distribution, its mean, median and modal class
Cricket: a batter's scores grouped in ranges — is the median or mean the fairer 'typical score'?
Income statistics: why news reports median income (a few billionaires drag the mean)
Daily-wage and rainfall tables from the NCERT are real government-survey style data

questions.prompt: For the distribution — classes 10–20, 20–30, 30–40, 40–50 with frequencies 4, 8, 12, 6 — the MODAL CLASS is

options.diagnosis: Chose the class with the largest VALUES; the modal class is the one with the largest FREQUENCY, wherever it sits.
Identified the right class but reported its class mark; the modal class is the interval itself, and the mode (via formula) need not equal its midpoint.

questions.explanation: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency: 30–40 (frequency 12). Note that 12 is the frequency — a COUNT of observations, not the mode; and the actual mode, computed by the formula, is a value lying inside 30–40, not necessarily 35.

questions.prompt: A grouped distribution has class marks 5, 15, 25 with frequencies 2, 4, 4 respectively. The mean is

options.diagnosis: Computed Σfᵢxᵢ = 170 correctly but divided by the number of CLASSES (3) instead of the number of observations Σfᵢ = 10.
Stopped at Σfᵢxᵢ without dividing at all; the mean must be brought back to per-observation scale.

questions.explanation: Mean = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ = (2×5 + 4×15 + 4×25)/(2+4+4) = (10 + 60 + 100)/10 = 170/10 = 17. The unweighted average of class marks, (5+15+25)/3 = 15, ignores that the higher classes hold more observations — frequencies are the whole point of a frequency table.

questions.prompt: For a distribution, mean = 21 and median = 22. Using the empirical relationship, the mode is approximately

options.diagnosis: Swapped mean and median in the formula: computed 3(21) − 2(22); the median gets the 3, the mean gets the 2.
Continued the arithmetic pattern 21, 22, 23 — a plausible-looking guess that ignores the formula entirely.
Added mean and median; the empirical relation is 3(median) − 2(mean), a weighted difference, not a sum.

questions.explanation: Empirical relationship: mode ≈ 3(median) − 2(mean) = 3(22) − 2(21) = 66 − 42 = 24. The formula reflects that for moderately skewed data the median sits about a third of the way from mean to mode. Swapping the roles (3×mean − 2×median = 19) is the standard slip — anchor it as 'median gets the 3'.

nodes.title: Probability: The Classical Approach
nodes.description: When all outcomes are equally likely — a fair coin, an unloaded die, a well-shuffled deck — probability needs no experiment: P(E) = (favourable outcomes)/(total outcomes). This node counts outcomes carefully (including for two dice and two coins, where 'equally likely' takes real thought), uses complements, and locks in the boundaries: probabilities live in [0, 1], with 0 for impossible and 1 for certain events. It is the theoretical twin of Class 9's empirical approach.
learning_outcomes: Can compute classical probabilities by counting equally likely outcomes (coins, dice, cards, balls in bags)
Can construct the full outcome set for compound experiments (two coins, two dice) and count favourable cases correctly
Can use P(not E) = 1 − P(E) and identify impossible, sure and elementary events
Can explain what a probability statement predicts about long-run frequency, and what it does not promise short-term

misconceptions.description: Probability is a short-run quota: 1/6 means one six in every six rolls, and streaks change the next outcome.
misconceptions.signal: Expects the sixth roll to 'make up' a missing six; treats a number as 'due' in dice games and lotteries.
misconceptions.remedy: Simulate 6-roll windows en masse: the number of sixes per window varies (0, 1, 2...), while the overall fraction across thousands of rolls settles near 1/6. Vocabulary fix: probability forecasts the LONG-RUN share, and independent trials have no memory — each roll is a fresh 1/6.

misconceptions.description: Outcomes can be counted without checking equal likelihood: two coins give three outcomes (0, 1, 2 heads), each with probability 1/3.
misconceptions.signal: P(two heads) = 1/3; for two dice, treats the eleven sums 2–12 as equally likely, so P(sum 12) = 1/11.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand to the full ordered outcome grid: two coins are HH, HT, TH, TT — the 'one head' label covers TWO of the four equally likely outcomes. For dice, the 6×6 = 36-cell table shows sum 7 arriving six ways and sum 12 only one. Rule: count at the level where outcomes are genuinely symmetric.

misconceptions.description: Complements are optional or misapplied: P(not E) is computed independently, or the probabilities of any two events are assumed to sum to 1.
misconceptions.signal: Given P(king) asks 'how can I know P(not king)?'; assumes P(red ball) + P(green ball) = 1 in a bag that also holds blue balls.
misconceptions.remedy: Partition picture: E and not-E split the whole outcome set with nothing left over, so their probabilities MUST total 1 — but two arbitrary events (red, green) may leave room for others. Drill 'sum to 1' checks on complete lists only, and use 1 − P(E) as the fast lane for 'at least one' problems.

misconceptions.description: Probabilities can exceed 1, be negative, or be plain counts.
misconceptions.signal: Reports P = 4 for four kings; offers −0.2 for 'very unlikely'; answers 1.3 without alarm.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the sanity band: every probability lands in [0, 1], with the endpoints reserved for impossible and certain. Any answer outside the band is self-refuting — train the student to treat it like a negative length: stop and re-examine, don't report.

real_world_hooks: The toss in cricket: 50-50 — but is winning 5 tosses in a row evidence of cheating?
Ludo and snakes-and-ladders: the real waiting time for a six
A deck of 52: probabilities behind card games and magic tricks
Why lotteries are a 'tax on hopeful arithmetic': tiny favourable counts over astronomical totals

questions.prompt: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. The probability that it is a king is

options.diagnosis: Counted only one king; a deck holds four kings (one per suit), so the favourable count is 4.
Confused with the probability of drawing a particular SUIT (13/52); kings number 4, not 13.

questions.explanation: P(king) = favourable/total = 4/52 = 1/13. There are four kings among 52 equally likely cards. 12/13 is P(NOT a king) — the complement, useful but not what was asked.

questions.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed together. The probability of getting two heads is

options.diagnosis: Used the single-coin probability without combining the two coins; the second coin halves it again: ½ × ½ = ¼.
Counted HH, HT and TH all as favourable — reading the question as 'at least one head' instead of 'two heads'; only HH qualifies.

questions.explanation: The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT — four of them, one favourable, so P = 1/4. The popular 1/3 comes from listing '0 heads, 1 head, 2 heads' as three outcomes: but 'one head' happens TWO ways (HT and TH), so those three labels are not equally likely.

questions.prompt: A fair die has P(six) = 1/6. Which statement correctly interprets this?

options.text: Over a very large number of rolls, the fraction of sixes will settle close to 1/6
In every 6 rolls, exactly one six will appear
If five rolls produce no six, the sixth roll must produce one
The probability changes after each roll until a six appears
options.diagnosis: Attributes memory to the die; each roll is independent and carries the same fresh 1/6 regardless of history.

questions.explanation: Probability describes long-run relative frequency (and the symmetry of one roll) — it promises nothing about any particular window of six rolls: zero, one, two or even more sixes can occur. The die has no memory, so no roll is ever 'due'; the chance is 1/6 on every single roll, always.
